doc.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011

title: Union pay scales for arranging, copying and guitar pedals
summary: Four-bar-page arranging rates, higher copyist pay, transposition and effects pedal premiums in the LA union.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: This is another interesting story. In the LA union, especially at that time, you got paid for writing an arrangement based on the so-called four bar page. So if you had a four piece thing or a whole orchestra, four bars, there was a rate for it. Right? So it could be anywhere from $4.75 for a rhythm section thing, to maybe $20 for a four bar page for a full orchestra or whatever. So whatever those rates were. And then you’d multiply those numbers and that’s what you got paid as an arranger. The copyist, however, got paid way more than that, double and triple. Because first of all you give them a score in concert and he’s got to transpose it, he’s got to write it and his penmanship had to be absolutely wonderful. I mean if you’ve seen the way I write my name you won’t want me copying any of your charts. And again, pre-Finale, pre-everything, so it had to be written just right. And then these guys got much more money for copying than the guy who actually wrote the chart. So there were times when we had to do something and the manager would say “well look we’ve got plenty of time, you want to do the copying yourself and make the extra bucks?” I said “yeah, sure.” Right. And so I would, with a felt-tipped pen, you know, try to copy, very, very slowly and try to make it look good. Well if you’re copying — our bands were basically big band style, we had four trumpets, three trombones, five saxes, rhythm section. Each one of those little parts copied by hand, you know, to somebody that’s not a good copyist — so I did that once or twice. And I said I’m not doing this again. So I’ll lose the money, let the copyist do it. And you know what else about copyists, they were so good, we did some recording sessions where we thought things were going to be in a certain key but the copyists were there anyway in another room at a table. And at some point they decided well let’s change the key to this thing. So they’d say “okay, hang on, take a half hour break.” And these dudes would be in there with the score and they’d say “up a minor third.” “Right.” And these guys would cook. And it looked wonderful. And there were a few parts they could put on onionskin and just xerox, but most of the other ones they had to write out one at a time. So that’s how fast they were. Now with the computer, a key change — in fact the union in Los Angeles, there used to be, if they asked you to transpose on site there was a certain scale for that.

There was a different scale for transposition on site. So let’s say you got the chart there and they say “well it’s just a little low, can you bring it up a whole step?” “Okay, I can do that.” And so they would pay you more because you transposed. for, for guitar players. If you had to use various pedals, so if you had the wah wah pedal, if you had the distortion pedal, you know, it was a little bit more money for having those things if they called for them.
Is that because — maybe it’s both — they’re paying you for the skill to use them, but also that you made the investment to have them.

I think so. And the idea that there is a different sound. At one time the union was very, very strong, and they said “okay, you want this — you want classical guitar, that’s a different instrument than a steel string guitar.” Well, not really. You play it with your fingers. But anyway, so they got many little, and these weren’t huge jumps, but they were enough so that it made a little bit of difference.
I don’t think the Utica musicians union ever had to go quite that far.
